newsitem.title: UK: Human rights group attacks police in N.Ireland.
newsitem.headline: Human rights group attacks police in N.Ireland.

text.p: An international civil liberties group accused Britain on Wednesday of fuelling Northern Ireland strife with repressive laws and police shortcomings.

Helsinki Human Rights Watch was scathing about the Royal Ulster Constabulary's handling of contentious pro-British Protestant marches last year and ensuing rioting, saying RUC police decisions had worsened matters.
The RUC rejected the criticism, saying in a statement the report "displays a degree of naivety of the very real difficulties in policing a deeply divided community".

According to the report, the police, the British government and other agencies failed to prevent the collapse of law and order and caved in to threats from Protestant hardliners who were allowed to march in two Roman Catholic enclaves last year.

"Despite RUC claims of being caught in the middle of disputes between (Irish) Nationalists and (pro-British) Unionists over the right to march', a series of police actions -- sanctioned by the government -- exacerbated the conflict," the organisation said in a report published at a Belfast news conference.

"These actions resulted in the effective submission of state authorities to the threat of Unionist violence and included the excessive use of force against peaceful demonstrators, the indiscriminate use of plastic bullets against both Unionist and Nationalist protesters, and a general failure to halt illegal activities such as the blockade of the airport and the establishment of illegal roadblocks."

The report was launched as Britain held talks with political parties and marching organisations to try to defuse tension and rebuild a peace process wrecked 16 months ago by the Irish Republican Army's abandonment of a ceasefire.

Accusing the RUC of "routinely abusive police practices", Human Rights Watch said that in holding centres operating under emergency anti-guerrilla laws "intimidation and harassment of detainees and lawyers representing them is commonplace".

It called for the scrapping of emergency legislation such as no-jury courts -- brought in to counter campaigns by rival guerrillas -- and a ban on anti-riot plastic bullets that have killed 14 civilians including seven children.

In a lengthy report into policing and human rights, some of the most contentious issues in decades of conflict that have dogged the British province, Human Rights Watch urged that the police be made more accountable.

"The British government has responded to the conflict in Northern Irelnd by imposing a draconian emergency regime that invests the RUC with expansive police powers to stop, question, search, arrest, detain and interrogate persons merely suspected of terrorist activity," the report said.

"Particularly with the planned resumption of multi-party talks in June, we urge the government of the United Kingdom to recognise that emergency laws such as those in force in Northern Ireland often serve to sustain political violence by creating an environment in which individual human rights are routinely violated," said Human Rights Watch/Helsinki.

The IRA is pledged to end British rule and reunite Northern Ireland with neighbouring Catholic Ireland. Leaders of its Sinn Fein political arm held talks in Belfast with British civil servants on Wednesday, the second in a week since London ended a ban on diplomatic discussions.
Britain says that Sinn Fein will not be allowed into multi-party talks, due to be restarted after a three month adjournment in Belfast next week, until the IRA calls an unequivocal ceasefire.
